assessment: P-104 describes recurrent aspiration pneumonia during nutrition care in a dialysis patient with parkinsonian syndrome, cognitive impairment and dysphagia. The report gives no ingredient-specific swallowing endpoint.

P-114 describes 82-year-old with Parkinson disease and COPD, recurrent aspiration pneumonia and ventilation. Four cans per day (1,400 kcal) of a lipid-predominant liquid formula via gastrostomy accompanied better nutritional and respiratory status without diarrhea. Formula ingredients and Parkinson outcomes are unspecified.
P-93 includes two Parkinson diagnoses among a mixed gastrostomy and PTEG cohort. The report pools feeding-route, texture and complication data without a Parkinson-by-food result.

P-108 reviews 108 gastrostomies including 26 with Parkinson disease and other neurodegenerative conditions. It evaluates procedural and nutrition context without identifying a particular orally consumed food or swallowing effect.

P-181 describes a 75-year-old with parkinsonian syndrome and refractory diarrhea after prostate cancer surgery. A pectin-containing REF-P1 viscosity adjustment during PEG refeeding preceded disappearance of diarrhea and reflux and later transition to Racol. Comorbidities, tube route and changes to volume and formula limit inference.

P-420 describes recurrent pneumonia in vascular parkinsonism, switching liquid to semisolid PEG nutrition and later discontinuation at home. The separate neighboring P-418 texture case does not establish Parkinson disease.

P-424 reports a 65-year-old with Parkinson disease and diarrhea on liquid gastrostomy feeds above approximately 700 kcal/day. Semisolid formula permitted approximately 900 kcal/day after a month, with loose stools at increments handled by adjusting dose. Product and ingredients were unspecified.

P-426 reports an older man with Parkinson disease, traumatic hemorrhage and severe aspiration pneumonia who transitioned from long-term parenteral nutrition to gastric feeding using GFO and small semisolid feeds. Mild diarrhea and fever occurred during transition and PEG reached 1,200 kcal/day after two weeks. The case combines route, volume, and several components.
P-442 includes one parkinsonian syndrome diagnosis among 24 PEG cases. Biochemical and early feeding observations are aggregate, with no diagnosis-specific food effect.

P-453 describes arginine-enriched liquid nutrition in a 78-year-old Parkinson case with severe pressure ulcers. The same page's agar and motility case is separate. No food-specific Parkinson swallowing result.

P-460 includes an 84-year-old woman with Parkinson dysphagia and hiatal hernia. Aspiration pneumonia occurred after a small amount of semisolid gastric formula; after jejunal delivery there was no reported reflux vomiting or aspiration pneumonia in the cases. Formula identity and follow-up interval are unspecified.

P-471 contains five parkinsonian syndrome gastrostomy cases with aggregate findings. P-472 is a separate severe infected-wound case with diabetes and a multi-extract carrot, Japanese pepper and ginger product. The shiso string spans a word boundary and the page supplies no 0725 Parkinson result.

P-609 describes Peptino and then Elental via jejunostomy after resection in a patient with stroke, Parkinson disease, dementia and denture ingestion. P-610 separately tests feed acid buffering in vitro. There is no food obstruction or Parkinson symptom comparison.

P-620 describes an 82-year-old woman with stage V Parkinson, hip fracture and low intake. Swallow examination identified no clear aspiration and the team combined PEG, two oral meals, medication and rehabilitation with adjusted textures. Named products from the adjacent case cannot be assigned to her.

P-705 compares an unopened frozen juice tube with standard ice-swab stimulation in seven dysphagia patients including one with Parkinson disease. Pooled coughing and swallowing rates were not significantly different; the authors did not identify the Parkinson patient's result or administer juice for consumption.

P-731 reports a 79-year-old Parkinson patient with variable intake on half portions of rice porridge, 1 saliva swallow per 30 seconds, and no immediate intake gain after a switch to dysphagia food. Oral intake returned after reliable enteral delivery of medication and other care. No food-specific causal estimate.
O-043 relates early intake to physical recovery after pancreaticoduodenectomy, which is abbreviated PD. O-041 is a separate glucose-control supplement study.
The PD abbreviation here describes pancreaticoduodenectomy in a study of postoperative enteral nutrition. The neighboring papers concern pancreatitis and surgical hydration.

Visually verified O-220. Katata reports 15 respiratory-deterioration choking events including five Parkinson patients and both inpatient events. Pooled causes are four mochi, four sushi or sashimi, two mandarins, one each beef, shiitake, rice and pudding, and one unidentified. The shiitake event is not linked to diagnosis, and choking events differ from longitudinal dysphagia severity.
PD is a code for 4 mL thickened barium in the comparative swallowing-test abstract. The page does not establish a Parkinson-specific food result.
The green-tea item is in O-239, a warfarin and vitamin-K intake study. Fatigue is reported in O-238 after gastrectomy, where PD is a surgical abbreviation. No Parkinson green-tea result.

The nutrition-support audit counts three Parkinson diagnoses among 53 patients and pools diet upgrades, route transitions and other outcomes. No ingredients or individual diagnosis-to-response links are reported.

P-331 at the Tokyo neurological hospital describes 15 stage IV–V Parkinson patients, with BMI declining in five under calculated nutrition. The proposed energy adjustment for rigidity, tremor or dyskinesia was still being evaluated. No diet ingredient was assessed.
The water-load discussion of suspended drugs mentions anti-Parkinson medication. The black vinegar tablet suspected liver injury belongs to a different 43-year-old man without Parkinson disease.
P-370 describes pancreatic enzyme and lipid therapy for post-pancreaticoduodenectomy malnutrition. The abbreviation PD denotes that procedure.

P-378 includes an 87-year-old with vascular parkinsonian syndrome and depression-related food refusal. Foods and supplements included jelly, chocolate, bread, ice cream and milk alongside broader care. The soy milk and oligosaccharide constipation report P-379 is a separate disability cohort.

O-166 abbreviates pancreaticoduodenectomy as PD. O-168 mentions postoperative fatigue in orthopedic patients receiving carbohydrate/arginine hydration. Shiso matched across the verb and determiner in 施行しその; no herb was given.

O-178 investigates swallowing correlates in corticobasal degeneration and progressive supranuclear palsy. The nearby choking prevention and stroke rehabilitation papers describe different patient populations.
P-065 discusses parkinsonism and swallowing difficulty in dementia with Lewy bodies. P-067 examines meal-service tea as oral care in a separate study. There is no Parkinson-specific tea outcome.
P-077 includes 12 Parkinson patients in a neurological nutrition-assessment cohort. It provides anthropometric context rather than a named dietary exposure and Parkinson symptom comparison.
P-090 assesses 32 Hoehn–Yahr IV–V Parkinson patients, with anthropometry and laboratory measures. Cilantro matched the given name Kanako written 香菜子; no herb or ingredient was administered.
P-146 includes Parkinson and related conditions in a pooled refeeding tolerance category. P-148 is a separate high-protein diabetic gangrene case. No ingredient-specific Parkinson data.
The page's PD exposure is pancreaticoduodenectomy in a protein-marker case report, without a Parkinson patient.
P-184 treats malnutrition after pancreaticoduodenectomy with digestive enzymes. PD denotes the surgery.
P-198 includes one Parkinson diagnosis in a cohort evaluating transition from gastrostomy toward oral intake. The adjacent A iito texture-modified food study is in gastrointestinal cancer.

P-338 case 3 is a 77-year-old woman with Parkinson who developed leukopenia and anemia after seven months of PEG. The three cases concern copper deficiency during tube feeding, without an oral food-specific Parkinson symptom result.
P-344 describes recurrent gastric distension after gastrostomy for dysphagia associated with stroke and parkinsonian syndrome. No particular oral food or Parkinson disease subgroup is assessed.

A stage V Parkinson patient appears in O-0065, a calorimetry and body composition case comparison. The neighboring O-0066 uses 5–10 mL oral syringe feeding in an 88-year-old with Lewy body dementia. Neither case tests a particular ingredient.
O-0075 concerns bowel resection after an obstruction in a patient with prior pancreaticoduodenectomy. PD-II identifies surgical reconstruction.
O-0146 lists Parkinson disease among indications for image-assisted gastrostomy. The outcome is procedural rather than a food-specific swallowing outcome.
O-0156 describes bowel injury during PEG placement in an 81-year-old woman with Parkinson dysphagia and recurrent aspiration pneumonia. The separate O-0155 concerns relief of PEG-feed vomiting.
O-0334 assesses tongue pressure during nutrition therapy in 39 older people and explicitly excludes Parkinson disease. No Parkinson bolus effect.
O-0370 studies body composition after stomach and pancreatic resections. PD denotes pancreaticoduodenectomy.
O-0380 compares early oral feeding with parenteral nutrition after pancreaticoduodenectomy, abbreviated PD.
O-0381 through O-0384 concern pancreatectomy, pancreaticoduodenectomy, postoperative fatty liver and tube feeding. PD is used for surgery.
O-0385 analyzes malabsorption after pancreaticoduodenectomy. Other abstracts concern esophageal cancer or surgery.
O-0395 evaluates mirtazapine for low appetite in a small mixed case series including Parkinson disease after colorectal surgery and Lewy body dementia. The tested intervention is a medication.
The PD cases in O-0510 had pancreaticoduodenectomy. O-0512 discusses fiber and zinc absorption in another enteral cohort, without a Parkinson comparison.
O-0576 reports vitamin A deficiency with rice balls and French fries in a child with autism and severe dietary restriction. No Parkinson disease or baked-potato airway endpoint.

O-0635 describes reduced retching and reflux after semisolid PEG feeding in an 80-year-old with Parkinson disease. The specific Heine Jelly used in O-0633 belongs to a separate study without a Parkinson-specific result.
O-0650 describes oral intake after home swallowing care in 43 mixed patients including Parkinson disease. Thirty-six resumed some oral intake, with no particular food or Parkinson-specific count.
O-0821 includes one Parkinson diagnosis among palliative nutrition cases. It pools clinical indications and routes without naming that patient's exposure or response.
A home gastrostomy report includes a Parkinson patient with dysphagia. The outcomes concern gastrostomy care, with no named oral food or attributable symptom change.
O-0958 administers Peptino after pancreaticoduodenectomy. PD is the operation, and the neighboring nutritional interventions have separate indications.

O-1078 prepares porridge, milk, salt, biscuits and separate vegetable juice as an emergency tube feed. O-1079 separately describes worsening parkinsonian syndrome and dehydration after the disaster. The ingredient recipe cannot be assigned to that case.

O-1205 describes a Parkinson patient with prior cerebellar hemorrhage, renal/nutrition complications and PEG feeding. The report concerns nutritional management and biochemical issues without a food-specific Parkinson outcome.

O-1220 includes Parkinson dysphagia and slow meals in a pressure-ulcer case treated with wound care and Abound. The outcome concerns wound recovery under several interventions rather than a change in swallowing after a named food.
O-1229 reports pressure-ulcer treatment in a patient with Parkinson and rheumatoid arthritis. The cocoa exposure appears in separate O-1230 and cannot be assigned to the Parkinson patient.

O-1235 describes complex wound and nutrition care in a bedbound Parkinson patient with bowel surgery and stoma. Neighboring supplements and wound cases do not identify a Parkinson-specific food effect.

O-1244 reports some roasted sweet potato and pie consumption during dysphagia rehabilitation after subarachnoid hemorrhage. The case is not identified as Parkinson and reports no choking from those foods.
O-008 examines immunonutrition in pancreaticoduodenectomy. PD denotes the procedure. Other abstracts concern esophageal or pancreatic cancer.

O-105 gives 2 cm cubes of sweet potato before bed to 31 postoperative esophageal or gastric cancer patients with reflux. Seventeen reported favorable outcomes, with substantial nonadherence among nonresponders. No Parkinson group or choking comparison.

O-171 reports vomiting with semisolid PG Soft via PEG in a Parkinson patient with severe dysphagia, malnutrition and pressure ulcers. Nutrition support and route changes included PEG-J. Neighboring named puddings and wound drinks are distinct cases.

P-016 compares 1 mL water and 1% Ajinomoto umami solution dropped on the mouth floor in seven dysphagic patients, one with Parkinson disease. Pooled 30-second swallow count rose by mean 0.36; time changes were not significant. No Parkinson-specific result or choking measure.
The gastrostomy follow-up includes one Parkinson case among five early deaths. It does not link any specific death cause, food or formula to the Parkinson patient.

P-114 follows weight after subthalamic stimulation in 27 Parkinson patients, while P-115 compares vitamin D measurements in Parkinson/DLB and atypical parkinsonism. Carnitine therapy belongs to a separate valproate case.

P-142 reports trace-element deficiencies during prolonged jejunostomy in a patient with Parkinson and cervical spinal cord injury. The neighboring semisolid-food mineral absorption experiment does not establish a Parkinson intervention.
P-197 through P-200 describe nutrition or complications after pancreaticoduodenectomy. PD denotes the operation.

P-276 reports a 76-year-old with Parkinson, dysphagia and chronic diarrhea during prior PEG feeds. GFO, Bifidobacterium BB536, ursodeoxycholic acid and incremental peptide formula accompanied absence of diarrhea and full enteral feeding by week eight. Adjacent lactosucrose constipation study has a separate population.

P-298 describes a man with Parkinson, dementia and heart failure progressing to three oral meals after professional oral care and rehabilitation. The adjacent radiation mucositis case used named adjuncts and cannot be pooled with him.
P-411 reports a PEG fixation-related event in an older woman with Parkinson, Alzheimer disease and aspiration pneumonia. No named food or swallowing response is attributed to an exposure.

Y-050 includes a man with parkinsonian syndrome and schizophrenia who tolerated peptide formula after ileus with concurrent laxative adjustment. Outcomes include stool interval, albumin and wound score, without idiopathic Parkinson or isolated food evidence.
Y-089 reviews 12 neurological nutrition/swallowing referrals, seven with Parkinson. Aggregate feeding routes and coordinated care outcomes have no ingredient-specific Parkinson result.

O-066 compares blood fatty acids in 12 independent Parkinson outpatients and 20 mild dyslipidemia comparators. DHA was lower (120.1 vs 149.3 µg/mL, p=.0037). No specific food intake or symptom intervention was measured; a larger same-team 2014 abstract has overlapping controls.
O-263 considers parkinsonian syndrome among comorbidities in a dysphagia grading study, with no named food or Parkinson-specific exposure result.
P-0190 describes a nutrition intervention 10 years after pancreaticoduodenectomy. PD is the operation.

P-0215 reports a 71-year-old Parkinson patient admitted for prolonged constipation with an obstructing colorectal tumor, then complicated postoperative nutrition care. The abstract does not isolate a dietary exposure.
P-0374 reports indirect calorimetry in a patient with stage IV Parkinson and rigidity under levodopa. The result concerns energy estimation rather than a dietary intervention or symptom effect.
P-0459 describes a child with autism and vitamin D deficiency whose restricted diet included rice and French fries. No Parkinson disease, baked preparation or choking outcome.
